attempts.name: g1a1
attempts.notes: I kept the stack-trace rule as the main signal and added three cheap signals that work on any project. The first is the test method's name split into words, such as "Missing", "Option" and "Exception". The second is the failure message and the string literals in the test body, matched against production lines and weighted by rarity across the production sources. The third is the test body's capitalized identifiers, matched to production class names. Production frames rank above these, and the top six picks are deduplicated so that no two land within 40 lines of each other in the same file.
attempts.outcome: better on training, not the best of its generation

attempts.name: g1a2
attempts.notes: I changed the localizer from a pure stack-trace reader into a scored ranking with three evidence sources. Production frames keep the highest weight, with earlier frames counting more. Identifiers from the failure message, the test method name, and the calls on the failing test line are matched against production source, weighted by how rare each match is. Final selection is greedy and spreads picks across files and methods, skipping any candidate within 40 lines of one already chosen, so the six slots cover more edit sites. I have not run this against the training cases, so the gain is unmeasured.
attempts.outcome: better on training, not the best of its generation

attempts.name: g1a3
attempts.notes: I added a second evidence source to the stack-trace rule. The new module also reads the failing test method's body and scores the production methods it calls, the production classes it references, and the class it is named after. Stack frames keep the highest weight, with a small decay down the trace. Candidates are ranked by score and then de-duplicated so that the six returned entries cover different 40-line windows, which helps with multi-site fixes. If the new scoring raises an exception or finds nothing, the original rule runs unchanged. I have not run this against the training cases, so the gain is unmeasured.
attempts.outcome: better on training, not the best of its generation

attempts.name: g1a4
attempts.notes: The refusal came from my use of `time` for the wall-clock budget. I replaced it with a deterministic cap on files and bytes read, and removed a dead branch from the previous version. The scoring logic is unchanged.

attempts.name: g2a1
attempts.notes: I added a one-hop call-graph signal, so production methods called by the called production methods also score, since fixes often sit in callees of the code the test exercises. I also added file-name token matching against the test name and report, and changed selection to spread picks across files (at most two per file in the first pass) because most misses lacked an entire file. The rest of the scoring, budgets and the 20-line suppression radius are unchanged. I have not run this against the training cases, so the gain is unmeasured.

attempts.name: g2a2
attempts.notes: The main change is a new signal for production code that the traces and test body never name. I added three generic signals: identifiers in the bodies of top production frames (fix sites often sit next to or inside the callee of a frame), IDF-weighted token overlap between the report text and both declaration names and file names (rare words such as `reset` or `subList` are strong evidence), and a file-level score that places a candidate at the class line. The rest of the greedy 20-line selection and the budgets are unchanged. I have not run this against the training cases, so the gain is unmeasured.

attempts.name: g2a3
attempts.notes: I added a message-driven signal and widened the diversity check. The failure message's rare words (for example "must be in order" or "invalid minus") are now matched line by line against production code and comments, weighted by how rare each word is across the project. Candidates are no longer restricted to declaration lines. I also changed the selection suppression radius from 20 to 30 lines, so the six slots cover more distinct edit regions. Production bytes read are capped lower to keep the scan inside the time limit. I have not run this against the training cases, so the gain is unmeasured.

attempts.name: g2a4
attempts.notes: I changed the scoring from declaration-level only to line-level. Every production line now scores by its overlap with the failing test's body identifiers, string literals, and test-name words, plus the frame methods from the trace, each weighted by rarity in the project. A line also inherits part of the score of its enclosing declaration, so edits in a method the test exercises can surface even when they are not on a stack frame. Stack-frame lines and the existing declaration and class signals are kept. The greedy selection with a 20-line suppression radius per file is unchanged. Work is bounded by file and byte budgets, not the clock. I have not run this against the training cases, so treat the weights as untuned.

attempts.name: g3a1
attempts.notes: The main change is in how production frames are turned into candidates. Previously only the exact frame line scored, so a fix elsewhere in the enclosing method was missed. Each resolved frame now also yields its enclosing method declaration, and the top frames pull in callees declared in the project. Selection is also more diverse: a candidate loses score for each already-chosen entry in its file, so the six slots spread across files, which matters because fixes often touch several files. Nothing here names a project, class or test. I have not run this against the training cases, so the gain is unmeasured.

attempts.name: g3a2
attempts.notes: I added a message-literal signal and a file-diversity rule to the existing localizer. Many misses cite a production file the stack trace never reaches, and the assertion or exception text often reappears as a string literal in production code. Production string literals that share at least two distinct words with the failure message now get a score, which can surface such files. Greedy selection also prefers an unused file before a second line in an already chosen file, so the six slots spread across files when the evidence allows. The rest of the pipeline (frames, declaration matching, test identifiers, budgets, suppression radius) is unchanged, so the behaviour on cases with clear frames should be preserved.

attempts.name: g3a3
attempts.notes: I changed the scoring to use the test's call graph and per-line evidence, rather than only declaration names. Test-side identifiers now come from the failing method, from test helpers it calls (one hop, half weight), and from test frames. Each identifier is weighted by how rare it is across production files, so names that only exist in test or framework code drop out. Production lines that mention those identifiers are scored directly, and each line also gets credit for its enclosing method's coverage and for its file. This targets the misses where the fix sits in a method the test reaches through helpers, or in a file that shares rare identifiers with the test, but where no production frame points. The rest of the structure (frames, suppression radius, file-named fallback) is kept, and reading and parsing are capped by a byte budget. I have not run this against the training cases, so the weights are reasoned, not tuned.

attempts.name: g3a4
attempts.notes: I added a one-hop expansion from the production stack frames. The earlier version scored only the frame lines and the declarations named in the test and trace, so it missed fixes in collaborators the failing code calls. The new pass takes the top production frames, reads the identifiers in each enclosing method, and adds the class or method declarations those identifiers name when the name is rare in the project, at a lower score than direct frame hits. The module also weights identifiers from the exception message against declaration names, and adds a weak fallback for sibling files in the directory of the top frame. Selection stays greedy with the same suppression radius. Nothing here is tuned to the shown projects: the rules rely only on stack frames, identifier rarity, and file layout. I have not run this against the training cases, so the effect on the 56/198 baseline is unmeasured.

attempts.name: g4a1
attempts.notes: I changed the scoring so that production code is judged by what the failing test and the trace actually touch, not only by declaration names. Stack frames from JUnit and JDK libraries are dropped before ranking. Method bodies are scored by how many rare identifiers they share with the test body and the report, using inverse-document-frequency weights so common words count little. Picks are spaced 40 lines apart within a file, matching the tolerance, so the six slots cover distinct regions instead of clustering near one hotspot. Files that share no identifier with the test or report are skipped to keep work within budget. I have not run this against the training cases, so the gain is expected from these changes rather than measured.

attempts.name: g4a2
attempts.notes: The main change is a file-level relevance signal. Production files are now scored by how many rare, project-declared identifiers they share with the failing test bodies and stack frames, weighted by inverse document frequency, plus overlap between test-method name tokens and file names. Declarations in the top-scoring files also get a body-level score from the identifiers their bodies use. Every file with a positive score contributes a candidate at its class line, so files the earlier version never considered can still reach the output. The 20-line suppression radius and the greedy selection are kept. I have not run this against the training cases, so treat the weights as untuned.

attempts.name: g4a3
attempts.notes: I added signals for the failures the current module misses most. Test assertion text and comments are matched against production comments and string literals, weighted by how rare each word is across the project. This targets cases like the `must be in order` and `minus signs must be leading` fixes. The module also matches issue numbers (such as `1385` or `582`) from test names and comments against production comments, and it matches rare identifiers used by the test and the stack against every production line, not only declarations. The innermost production frames also pull in their enclosing method, and production files named after the test class get a small bonus. Selection caps each file at four entries. I have not run this against the training cases, so the gain is unmeasured.

attempts.name: g4a4
attempts.notes: I added a lexical signal: production lines that share IDF-weighted tokens with the failure message and the failing test's method name now become candidates. Earlier versions only matched identifiers called from test bodies and declaration names, so they missed fixes whose edit sites share words with the message, such as `requiredOptions` for "Missing required options", or comment and string lines near the failing behaviour. Tokens are split on camelCase, and rare tokens weigh more than common ones. I also dropped JUnit and generic assertion words from the message tokens and cut the byte budget to keep the full scan well inside the time limit. The existing frame, declaration and suppression logic is unchanged. I have not run this against the training cases, so the gain is unmeasured.
